title: Production dead-letter queue filling up - thousands of undeliverable messages accumulating
description: Since this morning, the SYSTEM.DEAD.LETTER.QUEUE on the production queue manager has been filling rapidly. Currently at 48,000 messages and still growing. Applications depending on MQ messaging are reporting intermittent data loss. Business impact is high - the order confirmation and stock update flows are both affected.

worklogs.description: Initial DLQ examination. Browsed first 100 messages - all have reason code 2035 MQRC_NOT_AUTHORIZED. All messages are destined for ORDER.CONFIRM.Q.
Checked ORDER.CONFIRM.Q permissions. The consuming application's service account 'svc-orderconfirm' has PUT authority but not GET authority - this is backwards.
Investigated when the permission changed. Found deployment log from 02:15 this morning - a new deployment script ran setmqaut but used wrong flags.
Corrected permissions: revoked incorrect PUT from consumer account, granted GET+BROWSE+INQ to svc-orderconfirm.
Confirmed new messages are being delivered correctly. Now need to handle 48,000 backlogged messages in DLQ.
Wrote and ran MQ script to re-queue valid DLQ messages back to ORDER.CONFIRM.Q in batches of 1000. Processed first 20,000 messages.
Processed remaining 28,000 messages from DLQ. All messages re-queued.
Verified with application team that all messages were processed correctly by the downstream system.
Added DLQ depth monitoring alert at threshold 100 messages to prevent future silent accumulation.

comments.author: agent
comments.message: Hello, I am investigating the DLQ issue urgently. First step is to browse the DLQ messages to understand why they are being routed there. I'll check the MQMD header of the messages for the reason code. I'll update you within 15 minutes.

comments.author: customer
comments.message: Please hurry. The order processing team is saying new orders are not getting confirmations. This is a P1 situation for us.

comments.author: agent
comments.message: Update: All messages in the DLQ have reason code 2035 MQRC_NOT_AUTHORIZED. This means the messages are reaching their destination queue ORDER.CONFIRM.Q but the application cannot get them due to a permissions issue. The messages are not lost - they are sitting in the DLQ. I'm looking at the current permission settings on ORDER.CONFIRM.Q now.

comments.author: agent
comments.message: Found the root cause. The service account 'svc-orderconfirm' which runs the order confirmation consumer application has PUT authority on ORDER.CONFIRM.Q but NOT GET authority. The consumer needs GET to read messages. What's worse, it seems it has the wrong permissions entirely - it should not have PUT at all since it's only a consumer. This looks like a misconfiguration from a recent deployment. Can you confirm what time the deployment ran this morning?

comments.author: customer
comments.message: I checked with the DevOps team - they ran a deployment at 02:15 this morning for the order confirmation service. The deployment script included MQ setup commands. Is that what caused this?

comments.author: agent
comments.message: Yes, that is almost certainly the cause. Looking at the deployment script in your repository, the setmqaut command for svc-orderconfirm was written with -put +get flags but the + and - were swapped by mistake. It granted PUT and revoked GET instead of granting GET and revoking PUT. I am going to fix this now. The DLQ messages will NOT be lost - once permissions are corrected I can re-queue them back to ORDER.CONFIRM.Q.

comments.author: customer
comments.message: Please fix permissions first. We can discuss the script bug after - right now we need the flow running. How long to re-queue all the messages?

comments.author: agent
comments.message: Permissions corrected. svc-orderconfirm now has GET, BROWSE, and INQ authority on ORDER.CONFIRM.Q. PUT has been removed. I just confirmed with a test: new messages published to ORDER.CONFIRM.Q are being consumed by the application correctly. The 48,000 backlogged messages in the DLQ now need to be re-queued. With batches of 1000 messages, this will take approximately 90 minutes. The re-queuing process sends the messages back to ORDER.CONFIRM.Q maintaining their original order and content....

comments.author: customer
comments.message: Thank you. Starting the re-queue process is fine. The order confirmation team is standing by. Please send an update at each 10,000 message milestone.

comments.author: agent
comments.message: Milestone update: 10,000 of 48,000 messages re-queued. Application is processing the re-queued messages in real time. No errors so far. Estimated 60 minutes remaining.

comments.author: customer
comments.message: Order confirmation team confirms they are seeing the backlog being processed. Orders from this morning are getting their confirmations now. Keep going.

comments.author: agent
comments.message: Milestone update: 20,000 of 48,000 messages re-queued. Processing speed is consistent. I am also monitoring the ORDER.CONFIRM.Q depth - it is staying below 500 messages since the consumer is keeping up well. Estimated 45 minutes remaining.

comments.author: customer
comments.message: Good. One question - can we check if any of those 48,000 messages are duplicates? The deployment script ran twice before someone noticed the error.

comments.author: agent
comments.message: Customer asks about duplicates. Checking message IDs in the DLQ - MQMDs have unique MessageIds. The deployment ran at 02:15 (first run) and 02:18 (second run with same script). Need to check if any messages are truly duplicate or if they just represent two separate publishes by the sending application. Looking at MessageIds now.

comments.author: agent
comments.message: I examined the MessageIds in the DLQ. MQ assigns unique MessageIds per MQPUT call, so I can see the sending application did publish each order confirmation exactly once - no true duplicates at the MQ level. However, the DLQ does contain messages from both the initial 02:15 period and the 02:18 re-run attempt. The sending application seems to have retried failed deliveries, which is correct behavior. No duplicates to worry about.

comments.author: customer
comments.message: That is reassuring. The order confirmation service has its own idempotency logic so even if there were duplicates it would handle them, but good to know there aren't any.

comments.author: agent
comments.message: Milestone update: 30,000 of 48,000 messages re-queued. Still processing cleanly. I also want to flag something: I noticed there is no alerting configured on the DLQ depth. This issue was only caught because an application team reported missing confirmations - by then 48,000 messages had accumulated over 4+ hours. I would recommend adding an MQ DLQ depth alert at a threshold of 100 messages. Would you like me to set that up as part of this fix?

comments.author: customer
comments.message: Yes, definitely set up that alert. We should have caught this much earlier. What system should the alert go to - MQ's own monitoring, or can it integrate with our Instana monitoring?

comments.author: agent
comments.message: IBM MQ integrates with Instana through the IBM MQ Instana sensor. Once the sensor is configured, DLQ depth becomes a standard metric and you can set threshold alerts directly in Instana. However, that requires Instana agent configuration on the MQ server which may take more time. For today, I can set up MQ's built-in MQSC event monitoring to trigger an alert script when DLQ depth exceeds 100. This can be replaced with Instana integration later. Should I proceed with the built-in monitoring...

comments.author: customer
comments.message: Yes, set up the built-in monitoring for now. We will open a separate ticket for the Instana sensor integration.

comments.author: agent
comments.message: Milestone update: 40,000 of 48,000 messages re-queued. Only 8,000 remaining. ETA about 15 minutes.

comments.author: agent
comments.message: All 48,000 messages have been successfully re-queued to ORDER.CONFIRM.Q. The DLQ is now empty. The MQ event monitor has been configured to trigger an alert script when DLQ depth exceeds 100. I also corrected the deployment script in the repository to use the correct setmqaut flags - the PR is ready for your DevOps team to review. Can you confirm with the order confirmation team that all backlogged orders have been processed correctly?

comments.author: customer
comments.message: Confirmed - the order confirmation team has processed all backlogged orders. Customers are receiving their confirmation emails now. Outstanding work. The deployment script bug would have been very hard to spot on its own - thank you for catching that too.

comments.author: agent
comments.message: Great, glad everything is resolved. Summary: root cause was incorrect MQ permissions set by a deployment script with swapped flags (+put -get instead of -put +get) at 02:15 this morning. 48,000 messages accumulated in DLQ over 4+ hours. All messages successfully recovered and processed. DLQ depth alerting added. Deployment script corrected. I will close this ticket.

resolutionNote: DLQ filled with 48,000 messages due to MQRC_NOT_AUTHORIZED (2035). Root cause: deployment script at 02:15 set incorrect permissions on ORDER.CONFIRM.Q - granted PUT to consumer account instead of GET, and revoked GET. Fixed permissions (GET+BROWSE+INQ for svc-orderconfirm, removed PUT). Re-queued all 48,000 messages back to ORDER.CONFIRM.Q. Added DLQ depth threshold monitoring at 100 messages. Corrected deployment script in repository.

csat.comment: Exceptional response. Not only fixed the issue and recovered all messages, but also found the root cause in the deployment script and added monitoring to prevent recurrence. 5 stars.
